reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Seal coats are thin aggregate-in-asphalt coatings -- surface treatments, slurry seals, fuel-resistant sealers, and micro-surfacing -- used to seal/waterproof pavements and add wear and skid resistance in light-to-medium-traffic roadways and parking areas, without adding structural strength; DWG approval is needed for surface treatments on airfields due to foreign object debris (FOD) potential.
sections.body: Seal coats are one of several types of applications that consist of a relatively thin layer of aggregate cemented together with an asphalt (bituminous) material. The types of seal coats addressed in this chapter include surface treatments, slurry seals, fuel-resistant sealers, and micro-surfacing. Seal coats are widely used because of their low cost and usefulness in light to medium traffic roadways and parking areas. These treatments are normally used to seal or waterproof the pavement, provide wear resistance, and increase skid resistance. All seal coats are relatively thin coatings of material and do not add structurally to the pavement. Contact the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG) or their designated representative prior to using surface treatments on airfield pavements due to FOD potential. Surface treatments have FOD potential because they use aggregate particles 9.5 to 19 millimeters (3/8 to 3/4 inches) in diameter. Slurry seals and micro-surfacing use aggregates with maximum particle size less than 4.75 millimeters (No. 4), and fuel-resistant sealers use sand-sized particles less than 1.18 millimeters (No. 16). The major FOD potential from slurry seals, micro-surfacing, and fuel-resistant sealers occurs when sections of the seal are not completely bonded to the underlying HMA; individual aggregate particles (1.18 to 19 millimeters) are too small on their own to pose a FOD threat.
key_points: Four seal coat types covered: surface treatments (SBST/DBST), slurry seal, fuel-resistant sealer (FRS), and micro-surfacing.
Seal coats seal/waterproof, add wear resistance, and increase skid resistance, but add no structural strength.
Surface treatment aggregate is 9.5-19 mm (3/8-3/4 in); slurry seal/micro-surfacing aggregate is <4.75 mm (No. 4); FRS aggregate is <1.18 mm (No. 16).
DWG approval is required before using surface treatments on airfields because of FOD risk from coarse cover aggregate.
FOD from thin seals mainly occurs where the seal has debonded from the underlying HMA, not from individual small particles.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting among surface treatment, slurry seal, fuel-resistant sealer, or micro-surfacing as a non-structural pavement seal coat.

sections.title: Single and Double Bituminous Surface Treatments
sections.summary: A single bituminous surface treatment (SBST, also called "chip seal") is a bituminous material application followed immediately by a single layer of cover aggregate; a double bituminous surface treatment (DBST) applies two courses of bitumen and cover aggregate, the first coarser and thickness-controlling, the second keying into and partially filling voids in the first. Both are used on prepared base courses and new or old pavements; DBST provides greater wear resistance and minimal structural strengthening.
sections.body: A single bituminous surface treatment (SBST) consists of an application of bituminous material on a prepared surface followed immediately by a single layer of cover aggregate. "Chip seal" is a commonly used term for the same process. Double bituminous surface treatment (DBST) is similar to a SBST except that two applications of bitumen and cover aggregate are used. The first application of aggregate uses a coarser aggregate than the second application and usually determines the DBST thickness. The second application of aggregate partially fills the surface voids and keys into the aggregate in the first aggregate course. SBSTs and DBSTs are used on prepared base courses and on new or old pavements. DBSTs with additional layers are used to provide greater wearing resistance and potential structural strengthening (minimal).
key_points: SBST ("chip seal") = one bitumen application + one cover-aggregate layer.
DBST = two bitumen + cover-aggregate applications; the first (coarser) course sets thickness, the second keys into and fills voids in the first.
Both are used on prepared base courses and on new or old pavements.
DBST provides greater wear resistance than SBST and minimal additional structural strengthening.
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing between a single or double bituminous surface treatment for a prepared base course or existing pavement.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Introduces the two SBST/DBST material families covered in this section: the asphalt binder (cutback, emulsion, or asphalt cement per Table 4-1) and the cover aggregate (gradation per Tables 4-2/4-3), selected together for the intended traffic and climate.
key_points: Surface treatment materials are the asphalt binder (4-2.1.1) and the cover aggregate (4-2.1.2).
Both binder type/grade and aggregate gradation/quality are selected together for the intended traffic and climate.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting binder and aggregate materials for an SBST or DBST.

sections.title: Binder
sections.summary: The asphalt binder holds cover aggregate in place, bonds it to the underlying surface, and seals the surface against moisture and air; SBST/DBST binders are cutback asphalts, emulsified asphalts, or asphalt cements per Table 4-1, with ASTM D1369 offering an additional binder selection list keyed to aggregate size and application temperature.
sections.body: The functions of the asphalt binder are to hold the aggregate in place, bond it to the underlying surface, and seal the underlying surface to prevent the entrance of moisture and air. The binders specified for SBST and DBST are cutback asphalts, emulsified asphalts, and asphalt cements. The types and grades are shown in Table 4-1: cutback RC-250, RC-800, RC-3000 (seldom used currently due to environmental issues); emulsion RS-1, RS-2, CRS-1, CRS-2; asphalt cement 120-150 pen, 200-300 pen, AC-2.5, AC-5, PG 58-22, PG 64-22. ASTM D1369 also provides a list of binder materials based on aggregate size and expected temperatures at application.
key_points: Binder functions: hold aggregate in place, bond it to the underlying surface, and seal the surface against moisture/air entry.
Table 4-1 binder types/grades: cutback (RC-250, RC-800, RC-3000), emulsion (RS-1, RS-2, CRS-1, CRS-2), asphalt cement (120-150 pen, 200-300 pen, AC-2.5, AC-5, PG 58-22, PG 64-22).
Cutback asphalts for surface treatments are seldom used currently because of environmental restrictions.
ASTM D1369 provides a supplemental binder list keyed to aggregate size and application temperature.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the asphalt binder type and grade for an SBST or DBST.

sections.title: Selecting Type and Grade
sections.summary: Binder type/grade selection weighs climatic conditions, binder curing time, environmental restrictions, material availability, and the temperature/condition of the surface and aggregate.
sections.body: Select the type and grade of binder carefully. Consider these factors: climatic conditions; curing time of the binder; environmental restrictions; available materials; temperature of the surface; condition of the surface; and condition of the aggregate.
key_points: Selection factors: climatic conditions, binder curing time, environmental restrictions, material availability, surface temperature/condition, aggregate condition.
sections.applicability: Applies when narrowing the binder type/grade choice from Table 4-1 for specific job conditions.

sections.title: Cutback Asphalts
sections.summary: Rapid-curing cutbacks were historically used for surface treatments (RC-250 for cooler weather, RC-3000 for warmer weather), but environmental restrictions now limit cutback availability, driving wide use of emulsified asphalt binders instead.
sections.body: Historically, rapid-curing cutback asphalts were used for surface treatments. RC-250 was used when cooler temperatures were anticipated and RC-3000 when warmer temperatures were anticipated. Currently, environmental requirements limit the availability of cutback asphalts, and as a result, emulsified asphalt binders are widely used.
key_points: RC-250 was the historical choice for cooler-temperature surface treatment work; RC-3000 for warmer temperatures.
Environmental requirements now limit cutback availability, making emulsions the widely used binder instead.
sections.applicability: Applies when cutback asphalt is being considered as the surface treatment binder.

sections.title: Emulsions
sections.summary: Emulsions need freeze/settling/premature-breaking storage precautions but need little or no heating to apply; select emulsion charge type for aggregate compatibility -- anionic emulsions suit calcium-mineral aggregates (e.g., limestone), cationic emulsions suit silica-rich aggregates (e.g., chert, quartz gravel), and both adhere well to damp aggregate.
sections.body: Emulsions require handling and storage considerations to prevent freezing, settling, and premature breaking, but they are applied with little or no additional heating. In selecting the type of emulsion, consider the compatibility of the aggregate and emulsion. As a general rule, anionic emulsions adhere better to limestone and other aggregates composed of predominantly calcium minerals. Cationic emulsions adhere better to aggregates high in silica, such as chert and quartz gravels. Cationic and anionic emulsions both adhere well to damp aggregates.
key_points: Emulsions require little/no heating to apply but must be protected from freezing, settling, and premature breaking during storage.
Anionic emulsions bond better with calcium-mineral aggregates (e.g., limestone); cationic emulsions bond better with silica-rich aggregates (e.g., chert, quartz gravel).
Both cationic and anionic emulsions adhere well to damp aggregates.
sections.applicability: Applies when emulsion is the chosen binder and its charge type must be matched to the cover aggregate mineralogy.

sections.title: Asphalt Cements
sections.summary: Asphalt cements set quickly, holding cover aggregate well if not allowed to chill before aggregate placement, but require heated aggregate and high spraying temperatures, making cutbacks or emulsions generally preferable.
sections.body: Asphalt cements harden quickly so that the cover aggregate is held in place better than other binders provided the asphalt cement does not chill before the cover aggregate is applied. Chilling of the binder before applying the aggregate is one major disadvantage with asphalt cement binders. To ensure good bond, the aggregates are often heated when asphalt cements are used. Another disadvantage with the use of asphalt cements is the high amount of heat required for spraying. Because of the difficulties encountered with asphalt cements, carefully consider using cutbacks or emulsions instead of asphalt cement.
key_points: Asphalt cement sets quickly and holds aggregate well, but only if it has not chilled before aggregate is applied.
Aggregate is often preheated when asphalt cement binder is used, to help ensure good bond.
High spraying-temperature heat demand is a disadvantage; cutbacks or emulsions are generally preferred over asphalt cement.
sections.applicability: Applies when asphalt cement is being considered as the surface treatment binder instead of a cutback or emulsion.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Surface treatment cover aggregate must be clean, dry, single-sized, hard, angular, and polish-resistant (per ASTM D1139); flat/elongated particles and wet/dusty aggregate are avoided (moisture tolerance is higher, up to 3%, when emulsion is the binder). Tables 4-2 and 4-3 give recommended SBST and DBST gradations, cross-referenced to ASTM D448 size numbers; DBST combines gradation Nos. 1&2 (first/second spread) or Nos. 3&4.
sections.body: The aggregate has an effect on the degree of wear resistance, riding quality, and skid resistance of the surface treatment. Use only clean, dry aggregate fragments that are free from dust or dried films of harmful material. Ensure the aggregate has a single-size (uniform) gradation and is composed of hard, angular, polish-resistant material. Flat and elongated aggregate particles and wet or dusty aggregates are not used. Quantities of moisture up to 1 percent do not create a problem in warm weather, but dust prevents the adhesion of the binder to the aggregate. When an emulsion is used as the binder, aggregate with up to 3 percent moisture is commonly used. ASTM D1139 offers additional physical requirements for aggregates used in surface treatments. Tables 4-2 and 4-3 provide the recommended aggregate gradations for SBST and DBST, respectively, with correlating ASTM D448 size number designations. For DBST, gradation Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second spreading) or gradation Nos. 3 and 4 from Table 4-3 are used in combination.
key_points: Cover aggregate must be clean, dry, single-size (uniform) gradation, hard, angular, and polish-resistant (ASTM D1139).
Flat/elongated particles and wet/dusty aggregate are unacceptable; up to 1% moisture is tolerable in warm weather with asphalt-cement/cutback binder.
With emulsion binder, aggregate moisture up to 3% is commonly acceptable.
Table 4-2 gives SBST gradations (Nos. 1-3); Table 4-3 gives DBST gradations (Nos. 1-4), cross-referenced to ASTM D448 size numbers.
DBST combines gradation Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second spread) or Nos. 3 and 4 in a two-course application.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and gradation-checking the cover aggregate for an SBST or DBST.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: SBST/DBST aggregate and binder quantities are set per ASTM D1369, which gives typical application rates by treatment type, cites related ASTM measurement standards, and lists recommended asphalt/tar grades; similar guidance appears in Asphalt Institute Educational Series ES-11 and ES-12.
sections.body: The type and amount of aggregate and bitumen to be used for surface treatments is determined in accordance with ASTM D1369. This standard provides guidance on typical rates of aggregate and bitumen for the various types of surface treatments, and cites other ASTM standards that are applicable for measuring both bituminous and aggregate quantities. D1369 lists recommended grades of various asphalt and tar materials for use with surface treatments. Similar guidance is also available in the Asphalt Institute's Educational Series No. 11 (ES-11) and ES-12.
key_points: ASTM D1369 sets the type/amount of aggregate and bitumen for surface treatments and cites related ASTM measurement standards.
D1369 also lists recommended asphalt/tar grades for surface treatment use.
Asphalt Institute ES-11 and ES-12 provide similar supplemental design guidance.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining SBST/DBST binder and aggregate application quantities during design.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Field construction practice governs SBST/DBST success; equipment, surface preparation, and construction technique are all significant.
sections.body: Field construction practices determine the success or failure of a well-designed surface treatment; therefore, equipment, surface preparation, and construction techniques are important.
key_points: Field construction quality determines whether a well-designed surface treatment succeeds or fails.
Equipment, surface preparation, and construction technique are the three controlling factors.
sections.applicability: Frames the construction-phase controls (equipment, surface prep, application, control) for SBST/DBST.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: The asphalt distributor and aggregate spreader are the key surface-treatment equipment; the spreader is designed/calibrated for a predetermined, uniform aggregate rate and may be self-propelled (preferred, for uniformity and smoother operation) or truck-propelled.
sections.body: Among the equipment used in placing a surface treatment, the asphalt distributor and the aggregate spreader are important. Aggregate spreaders are used during the construction of bituminous surface treatments to apply the aggregate to the surface being treated. Design and calibrate the spreader to apply a predetermined amount of aggregate uniformly over the surface. Aggregate spreaders are self-propelled; others are propelled by the truck hauling the aggregate. The self-propelled aggregate spreaders are desirable because they allow for a uniform application of material and a smoother operation. Ensure calibration and operation of the distributor and aggregate spreader meet the specified results.
key_points: Key equipment: asphalt distributor and aggregate spreader.
The aggregate spreader is calibrated to apply a predetermined, uniform aggregate quantity.
Self-propelled spreaders are preferred over truck-propelled spreaders for more uniform application and smoother operation.
sections.applicability: Applies to equipment selection and calibration for surface treatment construction.

sections.title: Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Poor surface preparation shortens pavement life; repair soft/failed areas and remove loose material, dirt, and vegetation before placing the surface treatment, and sand or remove any bleeding surface first.
sections.body: Without surface preparation, the life expectancy of a pavement is reduced; therefore, repair all soft or failed areas and remove all loose material, dirt, and vegetation prior to placing the surface treatment. Also sand or remove a bleeding surface before construction of the surface treatment.
key_points: Repair soft/failed areas and remove loose material, dirt, and vegetation before placing a surface treatment.
Sand or remove any bleeding surface before construction.
sections.applicability: Applies to base/pavement surface preparation immediately preceding surface treatment construction.

sections.title: Application
sections.summary: Binder and aggregate application rates are critical: too much binder causes bleeding/low skid resistance, too little causes cover-aggregate loss; apply 5-10% excess aggregate (more wastes material and risks windshield damage), place aggregate immediately after binder, and roll immediately with a rubber-tired roller to seat aggregate and improve bond.
sections.body: Give attention to the application rates of both binder and aggregate. Too much binder causes bleeding or low skid resistance, and too little binder results in the loss of cover aggregate. Apply 5 to 10 percent excess aggregate, although too much aggregate results in a waste of materials and damage to windshields. Apply the aggregate immediately after the binder application to obtain a good bond between asphalt and aggregate. Rolling with a rubber-tired roller immediately after applying the aggregate seats the aggregate in the binder and improves the bond.
key_points: Excess binder causes bleeding/low skid resistance; insufficient binder causes cover-aggregate loss.
Apply 5-10% excess aggregate; more wastes material and risks windshield damage.
Aggregate must be applied immediately after binder for good bond, and rolled immediately with a rubber-tired roller to seat it.
sections.applicability: Applies to field application rate control and sequencing for SBST/DBST binder and aggregate.

sections.title: Control
sections.summary: Calibrate and check the distributor (ASTM D2995) and aggregate spreader (ASTM D5624) for specified application rates; keep nozzles uniform, control spray bar height for a double or triple spray-fan lap to prevent streaking, and construct at least one test section before full-scale application.
sections.body: Since the distributor and aggregate spreader are important for the successful application of materials, calibrate and check them to ensure that the specified application rate is obtained. ASTM D2995 offers a method for determining the application rate of asphalt (bituminous) distributors. In addition, ensure all nozzles are free and open, the same size, and at the same angle with reference to the spray bar to produce a uniform fan of asphalt. The height of the spray bar above the surface is important. A bar too high or too low produces a variable application across the spray bar, causing streaking. Ensure the height of the spray bar is such that a double or triple lap of the spray fan is obtained. ASTM D5624 offers a method for determining the application rate of aggregate transversely across the width of the spreader. A test section is another method to evaluate the construction techniques and the application rates required for surface treatment. Construct at least one test section before allowing surface treatment applications on a full scale.
key_points: Distributor application rate calibration/check per ASTM D2995; aggregate spreader transverse rate check per ASTM D5624.
Nozzles must be free, open, uniform size, and uniform angle for a uniform asphalt fan.
Correct spray bar height (double or triple spray-fan lap) prevents streaking.
Construct at least one test section before full-scale surface treatment application.
sections.applicability: Applies to quality control of distributor and aggregate spreader calibration before/during surface treatment construction.

sections.title: Slurry Seal
sections.summary: A slurry seal is a homogeneous, spreadable/squeegeeable mixture of asphalt emulsion, well-graded fine aggregate, water, and mineral filler that cures to a thin, sealed surface; it protects worn/weathered/cracked pavements, reduces skid/slip problems, suits roads, streets, parking lots, and bridge decks under light-to-moderate traffic, but is NOT used on airfields due to rapid aircraft-induced deterioration and high FOD potential.
sections.body: A slurry seal is a mixture of asphalt emulsion, well-graded fine aggregate, water, and mineral filler. These materials are combined in proportions to produce a homogeneous, fluid-like slurry. Ensure the consistency of the slurry is spreadable to be squeegeed over an existing pavement surface. A thick, sealed surface results after evaporation of the water and curing of the mix. When properly designed, constructed, and cured, the slurry seal improves the qualities of an existing pavement surface, but the structural strength of the pavement structure is not significantly improved. Slurry seals are used to protect worn, weathered, or cracked pavements from the adverse effects of weather conditions and traffic wear. With use of aggregates, the slurry seal is also used to reduce skid or slipperiness problems. Slurry seals have application to roads and streets, parking lots, and bridge decks. This type of seal coat is best suited for pavements that are not subjected to heavy traffic. Because aircraft normally cause rapid deterioration of the slurry seal and there is a high potential for FOD, do not apply slurry seals to airfields.
key_points: Slurry seal components: asphalt emulsion, well-graded fine aggregate, water, mineral filler, mixed to a homogeneous, squeegeeable slurry.
Improves surface condition (seals, protects, reduces skid problems) but does not significantly add structural strength.
Suited to roads, streets, parking lots, and bridge decks under light-to-moderate traffic.
NEVER applied to airfields -- aircraft traffic causes rapid deterioration and creates high FOD potential.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting slurry seal as a non-structural maintenance treatment for a worn or cracked road/street/parking/bridge-deck pavement (not airfields).

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: The core slurry seal machine is a truck-mounted continuous-mix slurry unit (the only recommended mixing equipment) plus spreader box, power broom, front-end loader, distributor, and pneumatic-tired roller; a revolution-counter method calibrates the machine's relative aggregate/filler/emulsion/water delivery per gate/valve/sprocket setting, and the mix is deposited via a squeegee box at a thickness equal to the maximum aggregate size.
sections.body: Various types of equipment are needed on a slurry seal project, but the basic pieces of equipment required include a truck-mounted continuous-mix slurry machine, spreader box, power broom, front-end loader, distributor, and pneumatic-tired roller. The truck-mounted continuous-mix slurry machine, which serves as a portable mixing plant, is an important piece of equipment. It is the only type of mixing equipment recommended for mixing a slurry seal. A slurry seal machine is used to mix aggregate, filler, asphalt emulsion, and water in the correct proportions and to uniformly apply the material to the surface to be sealed. The slurry seal machine contains storage for the aggregate, filler, emulsion, and water. Before use, calibrate and set the machine to deliver the job materials in the correct proportions. The machine manufacturer's instructions usually offer the best guidance for calibrating the slurry machine; however, a calibration method based on a revolution counter is applicable to all machines. By attaching a revolution counter to any shaft that is mechanically interlocked with the emulsion pump, water pump, fines feeder, and aggregate conveyor, the relative quantities of each of these components per revolution is determined for various gate openings, metering valve openings, or sprocket sizes. The materials are mixed and deposited into a squeegee box, which applies the slurry seal onto the surface at a thickness equal to the maximum aggregate size.
key_points: Basic equipment: truck-mounted continuous-mix slurry machine, spreader box, power broom, front-end loader, distributor, pneumatic-tired roller.
The continuous-mix slurry machine (portable mixing plant) is the ONLY mixing equipment recommended for slurry seals.
Machine calibration is by manufacturer instructions or by a universal revolution-counter method tied to the emulsion/water pumps, fines feeder, and aggregate conveyor.
The squeegee box applies slurry seal at a thickness equal to the maximum aggregate size.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and calibrating slurry seal production and placement equipment.

sections.title: Material Requirements
sections.summary: Introduces the four slurry seal mixture components covered in this section -- asphalt emulsion, aggregate (with its gradation subsection), mineral filler, and water -- each detailed in its own subsection below.
key_points: Slurry seal material requirements cover emulsion, aggregate, mineral filler, and water, each addressed in its own subsection.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying the four slurry seal mixture components.

sections.title: Emulsion
sections.summary: Slurry seal binder is asphalt emulsion, typically slow-set anionic (SS-1/SS-1h) or slow-set cationic (CSS-1/CSS-1h); quick-set emulsions need an experienced contractor given limited working time. Cationic slow-set cures faster (partly a chemical reaction) than anionic slow-set (evaporation-driven, so weather-sensitive); if the emulsion breaks on contact with the aggregate, change the emulsion or aggregate charge to reduce the electrochemical mismatch.
sections.body: The binder used in a slurry seal is asphalt emulsion. The emulsion is often either slow-set anionic (SS-1 or SS-1h) or slow-set cationic (CSS-1 or CSS-1h). The slow-set emulsions are best suited for slurry seals, but quick-set emulsions are specifically designed for slurry seals. The use of quick-set emulsions requires that an experienced slurry seal contractor perform the job because of the amount of time available for handling the slurry seal before it cures. Slow-set cationic emulsions cure faster than slow-set anionic emulsions because the curing process is partly a chemical reaction that expels water from the mix. Anionic emulsions cure primarily by evaporation of the water from the mix; therefore, they are greatly influenced by weather conditions. Low temperatures, high humidity, or rain slows or stops the curing process. Emulsion break; that is, the asphalt separates from the water upon contact with certain types of aggregates. If a break occurs, change either the emulsion or aggregate type. Aggregates have a slightly negative or positive charge. A cationic emulsion bonds better with a negatively charged aggregate and an anionic emulsion bonds better with a positively charged aggregate. Aggregates that have a minimum charge work with either an anionic or cationic emulsion.
key_points: Slurry seal emulsion is typically slow-set anionic (SS-1/SS-1h) or slow-set cationic (CSS-1/CSS-1h); quick-set emulsions require an experienced contractor.
Slow-set cationic cures faster (partly chemical reaction) than slow-set anionic (evaporation-driven, weather-sensitive).
Premature emulsion break indicates an emulsion-aggregate charge mismatch; correct by changing emulsion or aggregate type.
Cationic emulsion bonds better with negatively-charged aggregate; anionic emulsion bonds better with positively-charged aggregate.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the emulsion type/set-speed/charge for a slurry seal mixture.

sections.title: Aggregate
sections.summary: Slurry seal aggregate must be clean, crushed (angular), and free of plastic fines (which absorb excess emulsion, reduce wear, and cause premature break); crushed aggregate outperforms rounded natural sands (dune/river/beach), which have poor skid resistance and wear characteristics and are not used.
sections.body: Give close attention to the aggregate as well as the emulsion used in a slurry seal. Clean all aggregates, and crush the particles to produce an angular shape. Do not use aggregates that contain plastic fines. These fines absorb excessive amounts of emulsion, not allowing the required amounts of binder to coat the remaining aggregate. The fines also promote low-wear characteristics and premature break of the emulsion. Better performance is expected from slurry seals that are produced using crushed aggregate. Natural sands such as dune, river, and beach sands and other rounded aggregates tend to have poor skid resistance and wear characteristics and therefore are not used in slurry seal coatings.
key_points: Aggregate must be clean and crushed to an angular shape; plastic fines are not permitted.
Plastic fines absorb excess emulsion, promote low wear, and cause premature emulsion break.
Rounded natural sands (dune, river, beach) are unsuitable for slurry seal -- poor skid resistance and wear characteristics.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and qualifying the fine aggregate for a slurry seal mixture.

sections.title: Gradations for Aggregates
sections.summary: Slurry seal aggregate must be dense-graded (Table 4-4) so particles interlock; Type 1 is a thin crack-filling/sealing gradation, Type 2 is the widely used general-purpose gradation (voids, moderate irregularities, cracks, wearing surface), and Type 3 gives a thicker, coarser-textured seal sometimes used as the first course of a two-course slurry seal.
sections.body: Ensure the aggregates are dense-graded so that the particles lock themselves together. Table 4-4 shows the gradations for use with slurry seals. Gradation type 1 is normally used for filling and sealing cracks in a pavement surface, and it provides a thin wearing surface. Gradation type 2 is widely used, and is used to fill voids, correct moderate surface irregularities, seal cracks, and provide a wearing surface for traffic. Aggregate gradation type 3 assures a thicker seal and provides a coarser surface texture. This gradation might be used as the first course in a two-course slurry seal surface treatment.
key_points: Table 4-4 dense-graded aggregate gradations: Type 1 (thin crack-fill/seal), Type 2 (general-purpose: voids, irregularities, cracks, wearing surface), Type 3 (thicker, coarser texture).
Type 3 can serve as the first course of a two-course slurry seal.
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing a slurry seal aggregate gradation type (1, 2, or 3) for the intended surface condition.

sections.title: Mineral Filler
sections.summary: Mineral filler (Portland cement or hydrated lime) at 0.5-4.0% by weight of the total mixture addresses stability/segregation problems by suspending heavier aggregate and meeting gradation requirements, but fines/filler content must stay within gradation limits since excess causes shrinkage cracking in the seal coat.
sections.body: When stability or segregation problems occur, mineral filler at a rate of 0.5 to 4.0 percent by weight of the total mixture is used to solve the problem. When mineral filler is needed, Portland cement (PC) or hydrated lime (HL) is often used in slurry seals. The filler is used to improve the mix stability, that is, to suspend heavier aggregate particles throughout the slurry seal mixture, to reduce segregation of materials, and to meet gradation requirements. Take care to ensure that the fines content, including mineral filler, does not exceed the gradation limits. Excessive fines or mineral filler causes shrinkage cracking to occur in the seal coat.
key_points: Mineral filler (Portland cement or hydrated lime) is used at 0.5-4.0% by weight of the total mixture when stability/segregation problems occur.
Filler suspends heavier aggregate particles, reduces segregation, and helps meet gradation requirements.
Excess fines/filler beyond gradation limits causes shrinkage cracking in the seal coat.
sections.applicability: Applies when a slurry seal mix shows stability or segregation problems requiring mineral filler.

sections.title: Water
sections.summary: Water controls slurry seal workability; too much water causes a soupy mix with segregation or bleeding, too little produces a stiff mix that won't spread or perform; only potable water is used.
sections.body: Water controls the workability of the slurry seal mixture. Ensure the mixture contains the required amount of water to produce a smooth, creamy, homogeneous, fluid-like appearance. If more water is used than required, the resultant mixture is soupy, and segregation or bleeding of the mixture occurs. On the other hand, if less water is used than required, the slurry mixture is stiff and neither spreads smoothly nor performs. Use only potable water in a slurry seal mixture.
key_points: Correct water content gives a smooth, creamy, homogeneous, fluid-like slurry.
Excess water causes a soupy mix with segregation/bleeding; too little water gives a stiff mix that spreads and performs poorly.
Only potable water is used in a slurry seal mixture.
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning the water content of a slurry seal mixture in the field or lab.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: The slurry seal job-mix formula (JMF) sets optimum asphalt content from desired asphalt film thickness and aggregate absorption; water/mineral-filler content is set by a cone test, wear by the wet track abrasion test (WTAT, ASTM D3910); Appendix C gives a summary design method and worked example, but the JMF is only a starting point -- a field test section is used to adjust proportions to actual site conditions.
sections.body: The method of developing a JMF for slurry seals selects the optimum asphalt content based on a desired film thickness of asphalt and the absorption characteristics of the aggregate. The water and mineral filler content requirements are determined by a cone test, and the wear characteristics are determined by the wet track abrasion test (WTAT) as described in ASTM D3910. Appendix C contains a summary design method and an example problem for slurry seals. The method is intended to furnish a starting point for field application. Adjust the proportions of the mixture to field conditions; however, construct a field test section using the laboratory-developed JMF.
key_points: Optimum asphalt content is based on desired asphalt film thickness and aggregate absorption characteristics.
Water and mineral filler content are set by a cone test; wear characteristics by the WTAT (ASTM D3910).
Appendix C gives a summary slurry seal design method and worked example, intended only as a field starting point.
A field test section built with the lab JMF is used to adjust the mix to actual site conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when developing or field-verifying the job-mix formula (JMF) for a slurry seal.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Design
sections.summary: Slurry seal is low-cost but adds no structural strength and wears rapidly under heavy traffic; it fills/seals cracks, retards oxidation/raveling as a thin 6 mm (1/4 in) wearing surface, benefits from crushed aggregate for skid resistance, is weather-sensitive while uncured, requires traffic closure to cure (usually 6 hours, sometimes up to 24), suits only structurally sound, low/moderate-traffic pavements, and typically lasts three to five years, filling cracks and coating the surface to a depth of 3 to 6 mm (1/8 to 1/4 in).
sections.body: Consider these important factors before using a slurry seal: the cost of placing a slurry seal is relatively small, but this mixture does not provide additional strength to the pavement and does wear rapidly under a high volume of traffic; slurry seal fills and seals many surface cracks; slurry seals are used to seal a pavement surface to retard oxidation and raveling or to provide a thin (6-millimeter (1/4-inch)) wearing surface; skid resistance is improved if crushed aggregates are used in the mix; uncured slurry seal is adversely affected by changes in weather conditions; close treated pavement to traffic to allow the slurry seal to cure (sometimes as long as 24 hours, but usually 6 hours); slurry seal is better suited for a pavement subjected to low or moderate traffic because heavy traffic causes a rapid deterioration of the thin layer; only structurally sound pavements are suited for a slurry seal; design and application are important for meeting required job performance; generally, slurry seals have a three- to five-year life; slurry seals fill cracks and coat the surface of the pavement to a depth of 3 to 6 millimeters (1/8 to 1/4 inch).
key_points: Low placement cost but no structural strength added; wears rapidly under high traffic volume.
Provides a thin 6 mm (1/4 in) wearing surface that retards oxidation/raveling and fills cracks 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in) deep.
Cure closure is usually 6 hours, sometimes up to 24 hours; uncured slurry seal is weather-sensitive.
Best suited to structurally sound pavements under low/moderate traffic; typical service life is 3-5 years.
sections.applicability: Applies when deciding whether slurry seal is an appropriate treatment for a given pavement and traffic condition.

sections.title: Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Poor surface preparation shortens slurry seal life; remove loose material (including loose or flaky paint), dirt, and vegetation, treat cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in), then apply a light tack coat after cleaning to improve bond and reduce asphalt absorption by the old surface.
sections.body: Without surface preparation, the life expectancy of a slurry seal surface is reduced. Remove all loose material (including loose or flaky paint), dirt, and vegetation. Treat cracks wider than 3 millimeters (1/8 inch) before applying the seal coat. After the surface is cleaned, apply a light tack coat to improve the bond and to reduce the asphalt absorption of the old surface.
key_points: Remove loose material (including loose/flaky paint), dirt, and vegetation before placing a slurry seal.
Treat cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in) before sealing.
Apply a light tack coat after cleaning to improve bond and reduce old-surface asphalt absorption.
sections.applicability: Applies to surface preparation immediately preceding slurry seal placement.

sections.title: Application
sections.summary: Finished slurry seal surface texture depends on spreader-box lining condition, cured-slurry buildup on the lining/squeegee, and burlap drag condition; worn lining causes uneven thickness, and trapped fragments cause gouges/streaks, so the drag is washed/replaced and the discharge-chute mesh basket emptied/cleaned regularly; lumps/balling indicate inadequate mixing or premature emulsion break.
sections.body: The surface texture of the fresh slurry seal is affected by the condition of the flexible lining of the spreader box, fragments of cured slurry adhering to the edges of the lining or to the squeegee, and the condition of the burlap drag. Worn lining results in an uneven thickness of the seal coat. Fragments of cured slurry seal or aggregate particles caught in the lining produce gouges and streaks. Wash or replace the burlap drag as needed to ensure that accumulations or crusts of mix do not cause scars or streaks. Empty and clean the mesh basket screen that is hung at the end of the discharge chute. Check the slurry seal for lumps or balling, which is caused by inadequate mixing or premature break of the asphalt emulsion. Deviation of the mix from the specified gradation potentially results in a product not meeting required job performance.
key_points: Worn spreader-box lining causes uneven seal thickness; trapped cured-slurry/aggregate fragments cause gouges and streaks.
Wash/replace the burlap drag and empty/clean the discharge-chute mesh basket regularly to prevent scars/streaks.
Lumps or balling in the slurry indicate inadequate mixing or premature emulsion break.
sections.applicability: Applies to equipment condition checks and mix-quality monitoring during slurry seal placement.

sections.title: Joints
sections.summary: Make joints while the first-pass slurry is still semi-fluid/workable when possible; otherwise let the prior pass set and cure enough to support the spreader box without scarring, tearing, or scraping.
sections.body: Whenever possible, make joints while the slurry seal mixture applied in the first pass is still semi-fluid and workable. If operations preclude fresh working joints, allow the previously laid pass to set and cure sufficiently to support the spreader box without scarring, tearing, or being scraped from the pavement surface.
key_points: Preferred practice: form joints while the adjacent first-pass slurry is still semi-fluid and workable.
If that is not possible, let the prior pass cure enough to support the spreader box without scarring or scraping.
sections.applicability: Applies to longitudinal/transverse joint construction between adjacent slurry seal passes.

sections.title: Hand Application
sections.summary: Hand-squeegee application of slurry seal must avoid overworking, which prematurely breaks the emulsion before spreading is finished and produces a nonuniform mix with poor appearance and durability.
sections.body: Give close attention to spreading of the slurry seal mixture by hand squeegee. Overworking causes partial breaking of the emulsion before the final spreading is completed, which results in a nonuniform material that has poor appearance and durability.
key_points: Overworking a hand-squeegeed slurry seal partially breaks the emulsion before spreading finishes.
The result of overworking is a nonuniform mixture with poor appearance and durability.
sections.applicability: Applies to areas where slurry seal is spread by hand squeegee rather than a spreader box.

sections.title: Curing
sections.summary: Slurry seal cures by surface-water evaporation, by asphalt-aggregate deposition that frees water, or a combination, depending on the emulsion/aggregate pairing; a cured-looking surface may still be uncured below, so thorough curing must be confirmed before traffic is allowed.
sections.body: Slurry seals, depending on the emulsion characteristics in relation to the aggregate with which the emulsion is used, cure primarily by evaporation of water from the surface, by deposition of asphalt on the aggregate that frees the water, or by a combination of both. If curing is from the surface downward, the surface presents a cured appearance, but the material below possibly is still uncured. Therefore, assure thorough curing of the slurry seal before traffic is permitted.
key_points: Curing mechanism (surface evaporation vs. asphalt-aggregate deposition vs. combination) depends on the emulsion-aggregate pairing.
A surface-cured appearance can mask an uncured layer below -- confirm thorough curing before opening to traffic.
sections.applicability: Applies when judging whether a placed slurry seal is fully cured and ready for traffic.

sections.title: Rolling
sections.summary: Rolling a slurry seal reduces voids, smooths irregularities, and increases water resistance; begin only once the seal has cured enough to support the roller without pickup, using a rubber-tired roller.
sections.body: Rolling is advantageous in reducing voids in the slurry seal, smoothing out surface irregularities, and increasing the resistance to water. Begin rolling as soon as the slurry seal has cured to support the roller without any pickup of the slurry seal mixture. Use a rubber-tired roller for rolling the slurry seal mixture.
key_points: Rolling reduces voids, smooths surface irregularities, and improves water resistance of the slurry seal.
Start rolling only once the seal can support the roller without material pickup.
Use a rubber-tired roller for slurry seal rolling.
sections.applicability: Applies to the optional rolling step after slurry seal curing to improve density and surface finish.

sections.title: Fuel-Resistant Sealer
sections.summary: Fuel-resistant sealer (FRS) is a coal-tar emulsion + fine aggregate + water (+ occasional additives) mixture, batch-mixed and applied by hand, sprayer, or mechanical squeegee to HMA surfaces exposed to fuel drippage/spillage; coal-tar emulsion provides fuel resistance and fine aggregate provides skid resistance, placed thin (about 2 mm/1/16 in or less), adding no significant structural strength.
sections.body: Fuel-resistant sealer (FRS) material is a combination of coal-tar emulsion, fine aggregate, water, and occasionally other additives. These materials are mixed in batches and applied to HMA surfaces by hand, sprayer, or mechanical squeegee. Coal-tar emulsion binder provides a fuel-resistant surface, and the fine aggregate provides skid resistance. The FRS is placed in thin layers, usually 2 millimeters (1/16 inch) or less. Particle size affects the minimum thickness that is applied by squeegee. An FRS does not significantly enhance the structural strength of the pavement structure.
key_points: FRS = coal-tar emulsion + fine aggregate + water (+ optional additives), batch-mixed and hand/sprayer/squeegee applied.
Coal-tar emulsion gives fuel resistance; fine aggregate gives skid resistance.
Typical FRS thickness is about 2 mm (1/16 in) or less; aggregate particle size sets the minimum squeegee-applied thickness.
FRS does not add meaningful structural strength to the pavement.
sections.applicability: Applies to protecting HMA surfaces against fuel drippage/spillage where a fuel-resistant, skid-resistant thin sealer is needed.

sections.title: Areas of Application
sections.summary: FRS is applied to any HMA surface subject to fuel drippage or spillage, including vehicle maintenance and parking areas.
sections.body: Apply FRS to any HMA surface subjected to fuel drippage or spillage. This includes vehicle maintenance and parking areas.
key_points: FRS is used on any HMA surface exposed to fuel drippage or spillage.
Typical use cases: vehicle maintenance areas and parking areas.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying pavement areas that warrant fuel-resistant sealer.

sections.title: Considerations for Use
sections.summary: Use FRS only where fuel resistance is actually required (service life up to ~4 years depending on traffic/climate, shorter than asphalt-cement-bound surface treatments); low-turnover parking is better served by SBST/DBST or slurry seal; FRS protects/retards oxidation of the underlying HMA, needs 4-8 hours of traffic closure to cure, is weather (rain/freeze) sensitive while uncured, and is suited only to structurally sound pavements where mix design/application quality directly govern performance.
sections.body: Important factors to consider before using an FRS: use FRS only where a fuel-resistant surface is required; FRSs do not have as long a service life as surface treatments with asphalt cement binder, but they last up to 4 years, depending on traffic and climate conditions; parking areas with low vehicle turnover or low usage rates (therefore lower instances of fuel spillage) are better served with a single or double bituminous surface treatment or a slurry seal; FRSs provide a seal to protect the underlying HMA pavement to retard oxidation and weathering; close the pavement to traffic during the curing of FRS layers (usually 4 to 8 hours); uncured FRS is adversely affected by changes in weather conditions such as rain or freezing temperatures; only structurally sound pavements are suited for an FRS; mixture design and application are important for obtaining required job performance.
key_points: Use FRS only where fuel resistance is genuinely needed; it lasts up to 4 years, shorter than an asphalt-cement-bound surface treatment.
Low fuel-spillage areas (low turnover parking) are better served by SBST/DBST or slurry seal instead of FRS.
FRS layers require 4-8 hours of traffic closure to cure and are weather-sensitive (rain, freezing) while uncured.
FRS is suited only to structurally sound pavements; mix design and application quality govern job performance.
sections.applicability: Applies when deciding whether FRS (versus a surface treatment or slurry seal) is the right treatment for a fuel-exposed area.

sections.title: Material Requirements
sections.summary: Introduces the four FRS mixture components covered in this section -- coal-tar emulsion binder, aggregate, water, and additives -- each detailed with its own requirements in the following subsections.
key_points: FRS material requirements cover the coal-tar emulsion binder, aggregate, water, and additives, each in its own subsection.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying the components of a fuel-resistant sealer mixture.

sections.title: Coal-tar Emulsion
sections.summary: FRS binder is a coal-tar emulsion, typically specified to meet ASTM D5727.
sections.body: The binder material used in an FRS is a coal-tar emulsion. The coal-tar emulsion is usually specified as having to meet the requirements of ASTM D5727.
key_points: FRS binder is coal-tar emulsion, usually specified to ASTM D5727.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying the coal-tar emulsion binder for a fuel-resistant sealer mixture.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: FRS aggregate is natural or manufactured, angular, clean, and free of organic/objectionable material, meeting the gradation requirements of Table 4-5 (coarse, medium, or fine gradation type).
sections.body: Ensure aggregates are either natural or manufactured angular aggregate, are clean, free of organic and other objectionable material, and meet the gradation requirements in Table 4-5.
key_points: FRS aggregate must be natural or manufactured, angular, clean, and free of organic/objectionable material.
Aggregate gradation (coarse, medium, or fine) must meet Table 4-5's requirements.
tables: Table 4-5: FRS Minimum Application Rates and Corresponding Aggregate Gradations
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and gradation-checking the fine aggregate for an FRS mixture.

sections.title: Water
sections.summary: Only potable water is used in FRS, at a quantity set by lab testing before construction; high pavement-surface temperature conditions normally require additional water.
sections.body: Use only potable water in an FRS mixture. Determine the amount of water required from laboratory testing prior to construction. Additional water normally is required under high temperature pavement conditions.
key_points: Only potable water is used; the required amount is set by laboratory testing before construction.
High pavement-surface temperature conditions normally require additional water.
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning the water content of an FRS mixture for given field temperature conditions.

sections.title: Additives
sections.summary: FRS additives are polymer (often latex acrylonitrile-butadiene combinations) and silicon materials, added in the field or during the coal-tar emulsion's emulsifying process; additives must be compatible with the coal-tar emulsion used.
sections.body: Additives used in FRSs include various types of polymer and silicon materials. These materials are added to the FRS mixture in the field or added to the coal-tar emulsion during the emulsifying process. The polymer materials often used are latex combinations of acrylonitrile and butadiene. Ensure additives used are compatible with the coal-tar emulsion.
key_points: FRS additives are polymer (often latex acrylonitrile-butadiene) or silicon materials.
Additives are added either in the field or during the coal-tar emulsion's emulsifying process, and must be compatible with the emulsion.
sections.applicability: Applies when a polymer or silicon additive is being considered to modify FRS performance.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: FRS mix design historically selects sand/water/additive proportions from an allowable range per gallon of coal-tar emulsion; the current guide specification instead requires the final FRS mixture to meet two performance tests: curing time and resistance to kerosene.
sections.body: Historically, the design of FRS mixtures has been based on the selection of materials (sand, water, and additives) from an allowable range based on a gallon of coal-tar emulsion. The current guide specification requires that the final FRS mixture developed be required to meet two test requirements. These tests are curing time and resistance to kerosene.
key_points: Historical FRS design proportions materials from an allowable range per gallon of coal-tar emulsion.
Current guide specification instead requires passing two performance tests: curing time and resistance to kerosene.
sections.applicability: Applies to FRS mix design and the performance criteria the final mixture must meet.

sections.title: Application Rate
sections.summary: FRS minimum application rate depends on aggregate gradation: coarser gradation needs a thicker (higher-rate) application to fully embed the aggregate against traffic wear. Table 4-5 minimum rates: Coarse gradation 1.35 L/sq m (0.30 gal/sq yd); Medium gradation 1.0 L/sq m (0.22 gal/sq yd); Fine gradation 0.72 L/sq m (0.16 gal/sq yd). These are general-guidance minimums that vary with the sealer's actual solids content; recent research favors the fine gradation (thinner coating) where possible since it is less prone to age-cracking and gives a longer FRS service life.
sections.body: The rate of application of sealer depends, to a great extent, on the gradation of the aggregate used. The coarser the gradation, the thicker the application required. This ensures that the aggregate is embedded in the sealer and does not wear off under traffic. The rates given are for general guidance and vary depending on the final proportions (solids content) of the sealer that is applied. Table 4-5 gives the minimum application rate by gradation type: Coarse gradation, 1.35 liters per square meter (0.30 gallons per square yard); Medium gradation, 1.0 liter per square meter (0.22 gallons per square yard); Fine gradation, 0.72 liters per square meter (0.16 gallons per square yard). Recent research suggests that thinner coatings of FRS are not as susceptible to cracking with age; therefore, when possible, use the fine gradation (smaller size aggregate particle). This decreases the occurrence of cracking and increases the life span of the FRS.
key_points: Table 4-5 minimum FRS application rates by gradation: Coarse 1.35 L/sq m (0.30 gal/sq yd); Medium 1.0 L/sq m (0.22 gal/sq yd); Fine 0.72 L/sq m (0.16 gal/sq yd).
Coarser gradation requires a thicker (higher-rate) application so aggregate stays embedded under traffic.
Rates are general-guidance minimums that vary with the sealer's actual solids content.
Fine gradation (thinner FRS coating) is preferred where feasible -- less age-cracking and longer service life.
tables: Table 4-5: FRS Minimum Application Rates and Corresponding Aggregate Gradations
sections.applicability: Applies when setting the target FRS application rate for a chosen aggregate gradation type (coarse/medium/fine).

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: The finished FRS mixture must meet Table 4-6: curing time (firm set) 8 hours maximum and resistance to kerosene showing no penetration or loss of adhesion (both per ASTM D2939); sand added to the mix must not exceed 480 to 720 grams per liter (4 to 6 pounds per gallon) of coal-tar emulsion, since heavier sand loading is generally not fuel resistant and fails the kerosene test.
sections.body: The FRS mixture is required to meet the requirements provided in Table 4-6: curing time (firm set), 8 hours maximum (ASTM D2939); resistance to kerosene, no penetration or loss of adhesion (ASTM D2939). Ensure the amount of sand added to the FRS mixture does not exceed 480 to 720 grams per liter (4 to 6 pounds per gallon) of coal-tar emulsion. Sand loads of greater amounts are not normally fuel resistant and fail the resistance to kerosene test.
key_points: Table 4-6 requirements (ASTM D2939): curing time (firm set) 8 hours max; resistance to kerosene = no penetration or loss of adhesion.
Sand loading in the FRS mix must not exceed 480-720 g/L (4-6 lb/gal) of coal-tar emulsion.
Sand loads above this range are generally not fuel resistant and fail the kerosene resistance test.
tables: Table 4-6: Physical Properties of Sealer Mixtures
sections.applicability: Applies when verifying a finished FRS mixture against its curing-time and kerosene-resistance performance requirements.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: FRS placement uses hand-held squeegees, brooms, and other non-mechanical equipment for small jobs, or a truck-mounted batch-mix machine, squeegee blades, power broom, and front-end loader/fork truck for mechanical application; unlike slurry seal's continuous-mix process, FRS is always batch mixed, with tank depth tracked by a calibration sheet and dipstick.
sections.body: Various types of hand-held squeegees, brooms, and other non-mechanical equipment are needed on the typical FRS project. Depending on the job size, they are completed with only mixers sized to job size and hand-held squeegees; however, the basic equipment required for mechanical application on an FRS project includes a truck-mounted batch-mix machine, squeegee blades, power broom, and front-end loader or fork truck. The truck-mounted batch-mix machine is where the FRS mixtures are proportioned and mixed and then taken to the project site and applied to the pavement surface. FRS mixtures are always batch mixed and then applied, unlike slurry seals that are made in a continuous mix operation. The batch-mix machine usually has a manufacturer-supplied calibration sheet showing the number of gallons per depth in the tank. The depth is usually monitored with a marked dipstick. The squeegee blades apply the FRS material to the pavement surface. The power broom cleans the pavement surface prior to application. The front-end loader is used for aggregate handling; however, a forklift is often needed because bagged and manufactured aggregate is often used.
key_points: Small jobs: hand-held squeegees, brooms, and job-sized mixers; larger jobs: truck-mounted batch-mix machine, squeegee blades, power broom, front-end loader/fork truck.
FRS is always batch mixed, unlike slurry seal's continuous-mix process.
Batch-mix machine tank volume is tracked via a manufacturer calibration sheet and marked dipstick.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting hand or mechanical equipment for FRS mixing and placement.

sections.title: Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Remove all loose material from the surface before FRS application; clean and seal cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in) or containing vegetation.
sections.body: Remove all loose material from the pavement surface prior to application of the FRS. Clean and seal cracks wider than 3 millimeters (1/8 inch) or with vegetation prior to application of the FRS.
key_points: Remove all loose material from the surface before FRS application.
Clean and seal cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in) or containing vegetation before applying FRS.
sections.applicability: Applies to surface preparation immediately preceding fuel-resistant sealer placement.

sections.title: Application
sections.summary: Pour the mixed FRS onto the pavement and squeegee across; in hot weather, a fog spray of water before application aids bonding; apply a minimum of two coats, ideally each perpendicular to the last, to eliminate continuous full-depth voids, and place consecutive lanes while the prior lane's sealer is still semi-fluid where possible (otherwise let it cure enough to avoid scarring/tearing during the adjoining pass).
sections.body: After sufficient mixing, pour the FRS mixture directly on the pavement surface and squeegee across the pavement surface. In hot weather conditions where the pavement surface gets hot, applying a fog spray of water prior to application of the FRS material assists in bonding the FRS to the pavement surface. Use a minimum of two applications of the FRS material to eliminate the possibility of any continuous, full-depth voids in the FRS. When possible, make each additional application perpendicular to the previous one. Whenever possible, place consecutive lanes while the sealer mixture applied in the first lane is still semi-fluid and workable. If operations preclude fresh working joints, allow the previously laid pass to set and cure sufficiently so that it is not scarred, torn, or scraped from the pavement surface during the placement of the adjoining pass.
key_points: FRS is poured and squeegeed by hand or mechanical squeegee onto the pavement surface.
In hot weather, a water fog spray before application improves FRS-to-pavement bonding.
A minimum of two FRS coats, ideally applied perpendicular to each other, eliminates continuous full-depth voids.
Place consecutive lanes while the prior lane is still semi-fluid where possible, to avoid cold-joint scarring.
sections.applicability: Applies to field application procedure and lane-joint sequencing for FRS placement.

sections.title: Curing
sections.summary: FRS cures by water evaporation from the sealed surface; sunlight and warmer temperatures speed curing, with total curing time ranging 2 to 24 hours depending on FRS thickness and climate; FRS is never applied when freezing temperatures (below 0 degrees C / 32 degrees F) are possible within the required curing window.
sections.body: FRSs cure by evaporation of the water from the sealed pavement surface. Sunlight and warmer temperatures increase the rate of curing. Curing time varies from 2 to 24 hours depending on the thickness of FRS applied and the existing climatic conditions. Ensure FRSs are not applied when freezing temperatures (<0 degrees C, <32 degrees F) are possible within the required curing time.
key_points: FRS cures by water evaporation; sunlight and warmer temperatures speed curing.
Curing time ranges 2-24 hours, depending on FRS thickness and climatic conditions.
Do not apply FRS if freezing temperatures (<0 C / <32 F) are possible within the required curing window.
sections.applicability: Applies to curing-time expectations and freeze-risk scheduling for FRS placement.

sections.title: Micro-Surfacing
sections.summary: Micro-surfacing (also micro-texturing, macro-seal, macro-pavement) is a latex-modified asphalt emulsion slurry paving system -- latex-modified emulsion, chemical set-control additive, high-quality crushed aggregate, mineral filler (usually Type 1 Portland cement), and water -- originally developed in West Germany in the 1970s and used in the US since 1980.
sections.body: Micro-surfacing, also known as micro-texturing, macro-seal, or macro-pavement, is a latex-modified asphalt emulsion slurry paving system. This system was originally developed in West Germany in the 1970's and has been used in the United States since 1980. The total system consists of a latex-modified asphalt emulsion, a chemical set control additive, high-quality crushed aggregate and mineral filler (usually Type 1 Portland cement), and water.
key_points: Micro-surfacing is a latex-modified asphalt emulsion slurry system, also called micro-texturing, macro-seal, or macro-pavement.
Developed in West Germany in the 1970s; in US use since 1980.
Components: latex-modified asphalt emulsion, chemical set-control additive, high-quality crushed aggregate, mineral filler (usually Type 1 Portland cement), and water.
sections.applicability: Applies when micro-surfacing is being considered as a latex-modified slurry seal system.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: Micro-surfacing shares brooms, loaders, and distributors with slurry seal work, but mixing uses a multi-bladed twin-shaft pugmill and self-propelled mixing/placement vehicles with constant slurry-box agitation, either nurse-truck-resupplied or place-and-leave; a rubber rear seal strikes off on smooth surfaces, a steel strike-off forms an intermediate leveling course on rough surfaces, and V-shaped rut boxes with agitating blades fill individual-lane ruts.
sections.body: Some of the methods of mixing and application are similar to those of a slurry seal. Equipment such as brooms, loaders, and asphalt distributors are the same as for a slurry seal. However, other equipment required for mixing and application of micro-surfacing mixtures are different than those required for slurry seals. Mixing is accomplished in a multi-bladed, twin-shaft, pugmill mixer. Application equipment with constant agitation within the slurry box is required to achieve a uniform placement of slurry. Micro-surfacing mixtures are placed with self-propelled mixing and placement vehicles. These vehicles have bins and tanks to carry all the aggregate, filler, asphalt emulsion, water, and additives required to make the mixture. Two basic types of vehicles are used to place micro-surfacing -- those that do so with the help of nurse or resupply trucks and those that place and then leave for resupply. These vehicles have the ability to apply a fog spray of water to the pavement directly in front of the spreader box. The spreader box contains blades to continually agitate the slurry. On relatively smooth surfaces, the rear seal is rubber and acts as a strike-off (screed). On rough surfaces, normally a steel strike-off is used to form an intermediate leveling course, with another slurry then placed over the leveling course. Rut boxes are used to fill ruts in individual traffic lanes. These boxes are V-shaped, with the point of the V toward the rear of the box. They have two shafts with multiple blades on each side of the V to continuously agitate the slurry. The box is designed to push aggregate to the center and is equipped with two metal leveling plates and a rubber strike-off.
key_points: Brooms, loaders, and distributors are shared with slurry seal work; mixing is a multi-bladed twin-shaft pugmill (different from slurry seal).
Self-propelled mixing/placement vehicles carry all mix components and apply a water fog spray ahead of the spreader box.
Smooth surfaces use a rubber rear-seal strike-off; rough surfaces use a steel strike-off to form an intermediate leveling course.
V-shaped rut boxes with agitating blades fill individual-lane ruts and push aggregate to the center.
sections.applicability: Applies to equipment selection for micro-surfacing mixing, placement, and rut-filling.

sections.title: Material Requirements
sections.summary: Introduces the four micro-surfacing mixture components covered in this section -- latex-modified asphalt emulsion, set-control additives, crushed aggregate, and water -- each detailed with its own requirements in the following subsections.
key_points: Micro-surfacing material requirements cover emulsion, additives, aggregate, and water, each in its own subsection.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying the components of a micro-surfacing mixture.

sections.title: Emulsion
sections.summary: The micro-surfacing binder is a latex-modified asphalt emulsion, normally built on a cationic slow-setting, hard-base asphalt emulsion (CSS-1H per ASTM D2397), with latex polymer added at 3.0% by weight of residual material during the emulsifying process.
sections.body: The binder used in micro-surfacing is a latex-modified asphalt emulsion. The base asphalt emulsion used is normally a cationic slow-setting emulsion with a hard base asphalt (CSS-1H) as specified in ASTM D2397. The latex polymer is combined with the asphalt cement during the emulsifying process, at a rate of 3.0 percent by weight of residual material.
key_points: Base emulsion is normally cationic slow-setting, hard-base (CSS-1H) per ASTM D2397.
Latex polymer is combined with the asphalt cement during emulsifying at 3.0% by weight of residual material.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying the latex-modified emulsion binder for a micro-surfacing mixture.

sections.title: Additives
sections.summary: Liquid set-control additives are added during field mixing to control set properties; more additive is used as temperature drops, because it accelerates emulsion break/cure; obtain additives from the emulsion manufacturer to ensure mixture compatibility.
sections.body: Liquid additives are added during the field mixing process to provide control of the set properties of the micro-surface mixture. The amount of additive used increases with decreasing temperatures. This is because the additive acts to cause the emulsion to break or cure faster. Obtain these additives from the emulsion manufacturer to assure compatibility with all components of the mixture.
key_points: Liquid set-control additives are field-added to control emulsion break/cure speed.
More additive is needed as temperature decreases, since it speeds emulsion break/cure.
Additives should be obtained from the emulsion manufacturer to ensure compatibility with the mixture.
sections.applicability: Applies when adjusting micro-surfacing set-control additive dosage for cold-weather placement.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Micro-surfacing aggregate must be a high-quality, 100% crushed material (granite, flint, slag, limestone, basalt, chert, or gravel have all been used) meeting Table 4-7's Type 2 or Type 3 gradation -- the same gradation series as slurry seal (Table 4-4) minus the finest Type 1; mineral filler (non-air-entrained Portland cement, hydrated lime, or another mineral additive) is added, set by lab testing and normally capped at 3.0% of aggregate weight, to reduce segregation and tune the cure rate.
sections.body: Ensure the aggregate used is a high-quality, 100 percent crushed aggregate. Aggregates previously used for micro-texturing include granite, flint, slag, limestone, basalt, chert, and gravel. The aggregate is required to meet one of the gradation types listed in Table 4-7. The gradations used for micro-surfacing are the same as those of an asphalt slurry seal, except that type 1, the finest gradation used for a slurry seal (Table 4-4), is not used for micro-surfacing. Mineral filler is added to the mixture to obtain the desired dispersion (reduce segregation) and working characteristics (speed-up or slow-down the rate of cure of the system) of the micro-surfaced mixture. Determine the amount of mineral filler added from laboratory testing, normally not to exceed 3.0 percent of the weight of the aggregate. Mineral filler is non-air entrained Portland cement, hydrated lime, or another mineral additive.
key_points: Aggregate must be high-quality, 100% crushed (granite, flint, slag, limestone, basalt, chert, or gravel have all been used).
Table 4-7 gives Type 2 and Type 3 gradations -- the same series as slurry seal Table 4-4, but Type 1 (finest) is excluded for micro-surfacing.
Mineral filler (non-air-entrained Portland cement, hydrated lime, or similar) is set by lab testing, normally capped at 3.0% of aggregate weight.
Mineral filler reduces segregation and tunes the mixture's cure rate.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the crushed aggregate gradation and mineral filler content for micro-surfacing.

sections.title: Water
sections.summary: Micro-surfacing uses potable water free of soluble salts or other harmful material, limited to the amount needed for the desired mixture consistency; required water increases slightly with increasing temperature.
sections.body: Use potable water free of soluble salts or any other harmful materials. Limit the amount of water used to that required to produce a mixture of the desired consistency. The amount of water required increases slightly with increasing temperatures.
key_points: Water must be potable and free of soluble salts or other harmful materials.
Water quantity is limited to that needed for the desired mix consistency; slightly more is needed as temperature rises.
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning the water content of a micro-surfacing mixture.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: No military-specific micro-surfacing mix-design method exists; the recommended procedure follows the International Slurry Surfacing Association (ISSA) approach in three parts: (1) material evaluation against 4-5.2 requirements, (2) mixing/application-characteristic testing (water, filler, additives) via trial mixes to set optimum asphalt content, and (3) performance-related testing for long-term behavior; ASTM D6372 covers standard micro-surfacing design/testing/construction practice.
sections.body: A method of mix design for military pavements has not been developed. Instead, procedures developed by the International Slurry Surfacing Association (ISSA) are recommended for use and are detailed here. These procedures are broken down into three parts. The first is the evaluation of materials to verify that they meet the requirements described in section 4-5.2. These materials include the aggregates and the polymer-modified asphalt cement. The second part involves testing the effects of mixing and application characteristics, water content, filler, and additives, and determining the optimum asphalt content through the preparation of trial mixes. The third part involves performance-related tests on the mixture to ensure good long-term performance. ASTM D6372 provides information on standard practices in the design, testing, and construction of micro-surfacing.
key_points: No dedicated military mix-design method exists; ISSA procedures are recommended instead.
Part 1: verify materials meet section 4-5.2 requirements (aggregates, polymer-modified asphalt cement).
Part 2: trial mixes test mixing/application characteristics (water, filler, additives) and set optimum asphalt content.
Part 3: performance-related tests confirm good long-term performance; ASTM D6372 covers standard design/testing/construction practice.
sections.applicability: Applies to the overall micro-surfacing mix design process (materials, trial mixes, performance testing).

sections.title: Mix Characteristics
sections.summary: Trial mixes at constant asphalt-emulsion content with incremental mineral-filler changes set optimum filler content and check compatibility/wet-cohesion; once filler content is fixed, further trial mixes at constant filler with incremental emulsion-content changes refine the mix. Cohesion testing (4-5.3.1.1) and stripping testing (4-5.3.1.2) are the key evaluation tools.
sections.body: Trial mixes are used to determine if the emulsion and aggregate are compatible, if a mineral filler or field control additive is needed, and if used, the concentration and the range of water that produces homogeneous mixtures. Trial mixes are also prepared to determine the optimum filler content and the effects of mineral filler on wet cohesion. These mixes are prepared with constant asphalt emulsion contents and incremental changes in the amount of mineral filler, usually either hydrated lime or Portland cement. Once the desirable mineral filler content has been determined, trial mixes are again prepared, this time keeping the mineral filler content constant and making incremental changes in the asphalt emulsion content.
key_points: Trial mixes at constant emulsion content, incremental mineral filler, set optimum filler content and evaluate wet cohesion.
Once filler content is fixed, trial mixes at constant filler with incremental emulsion content refine the asphalt content.
Trial mixes also confirm emulsion-aggregate compatibility and the water range giving a homogeneous mixture.
sections.applicability: Applies to the trial-mix procedure used to fix mineral filler content and refine asphalt emulsion content.

sections.title: Cohesion Test (ISSA Technical Bulletin 139 (TB-139))
sections.summary: The ISSA TB-139 cohesion test (a power-steering-simulator torque test on a loaded rubber foot) classifies set/traffic time: "quick set" = 12-13 kg/cm (67.1-72.6 lb/in) torque within 20-30 minutes (the set/water-resistant/non-remixable point); "quick traffic" = 20-21 kg/cm (111.9-117.6 lb/in) within 60 minutes (sufficient cohesion for rolling traffic); all micro-surfacing mixtures are designed as quick-set, quick-traffic systems. Figure 4-1 classifies mix systems by cohesion curve; Figure 4-2 ("Benedict Curve") plots cohesion vs. incremental mineral filler addition to find the optimum filler content (highest cohesion value) and gauge the mix's sensitivity to filler variation.
sections.body: The cohesion test is the method used to classify the set and traffic time of micro-surfacing systems. The cohesion tester is a power steering simulator that measures the torque required to tear apart a 6- or 8-millimeter-thick (0.236- or 0.315-inch-thick) by 60-millimeter (2.36-inch) in diameter specimen under the action of a 32-millimeter-diameter (1.26-inch-diameter) rubber foot loaded to 200 kilopascals (4,177 pounds per square foot). A system is defined as "quick set" if it develops a torque value of 12 to 13 kilograms per centimeter (67.1 to 72.6 pounds per inch) within 20 to 30 minutes. A torque of 12 to 13 kilograms per centimeter (67.1 to 72.6 pounds per inch) is considered the cohesion value at which the mixture is set, water-resistant, and cannot be remixed. A system is defined as "quick traffic" if the mixture develops 20 to 21 kilograms per centimeter (111.9 to 117.6 pounds per inch) torque within 60 minutes. At 20 to 21 kilograms per centimeter (111.9 to 117.6 pounds per inch), sufficient cohesion has developed to allow rolling traffic. Figure 4-1 provides a method to classify various slurry seals and micro-surfacing systems. All micro-surfacing mixtures are designed as quick set, quick traffic systems. Cohesion test results are also used to optimize mineral filler by the use of the "Benedict Curve" (see Figure 4-2), in which the effect of an incremental addition of mineral filler versus cohesion is plotted. The optimum filler content is the value that gives the highest cohesion value. The shape of the curve shows the sensitivity of the system to changes in mineral filler.
