This helps determine the range of mineral filler that gives acceptable laboratory results.
key_points: Cohesion tester: power-steering-simulator torque on a 32-mm rubber foot (200 kPa) against a 6-8 mm thick, 60 mm diameter specimen.
"Quick set" = 12-13 kg/cm (67.1-72.6 lb/in) torque within 20-30 min -- the set/water-resistant/non-remixable point.
"Quick traffic" = 20-21 kg/cm (111.9-117.6 lb/in) torque within 60 min -- sufficient cohesion for rolling traffic.
All micro-surfacing mixtures are designed as quick-set, quick-traffic systems; Figure 4-1 classifies systems by cohesion curve.
The "Benedict Curve" (Figure 4-2) plots cohesion vs. incremental mineral filler to find the optimum filler content (highest cohesion) and its sensitivity range.
figures: Figure 4-1: Classification of Mix Systems by Cohesion Test Curves
Figure 4-2: Mineral Filler Content Optimization "Benedict Curve"
sections.applicability: Applies when classifying a micro-surfacing/slurry seal system's set/traffic time and optimizing mineral filler content via cohesion testing.

sections.title: Stripping
sections.summary: Stripping potential is evaluated with the Wet Stripping Test (ISSA TB-114) and Boiling Test (ISSA TB-149); the Wet Stripping Test boils 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) cured cohesion specimens in water for 3 minutes and checks asphalt-aggregate adhesion, with coating retention >=90% passing, 75-90% marginal, and <75% failing; either test also serves as an early compatibility indicator.
sections.body: Two tests used to evaluate the potential for stripping are: the Wet Stripping Test (ISSA TB-114) and the Boiling Test (ISSA TB-149). The Wet Stripping Test is performed on 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) cured cohesion specimens that are boiled in water for 3 minutes to determine the asphalt adhesion to the aggregate. A coating retention of 90 percent or greater is considered meeting required specifications, with 75 to 90 percent being marginal and less than 75 percent not meeting required specifications. The Boiling Test is similar to the Wet Stripping Test. Either test is also used as an early compatibility indicator test.
key_points: Wet Stripping Test (ISSA TB-114): boils 60 C (140 F) cured cohesion specimens for 3 minutes to check asphalt-aggregate adhesion.
Coating retention pass/marginal/fail thresholds: >=90% pass, 75-90% marginal, <75% fail.
Boiling Test (ISSA TB-149) is a similar method; either test also serves as an early emulsion-aggregate compatibility indicator.
sections.applicability: Applies when screening a micro-surfacing emulsion-aggregate combination for stripping (adhesion loss) potential.

sections.title: Determination of Optimum Asphalt Content
sections.summary: Optimum asphalt cement content is determined by ISSA test procedures, a modified Marshall procedure, or (in a few states) the Hveem stability test.
sections.body: There are several ways to determine the optimum asphalt cement content. One way is to use ISSA test procedures, and another is to use a modified Marshall procedure. A few states also specify requirements for Hveem stability test.
key_points: Optimum asphalt content methods: ISSA test procedures, modified Marshall procedure, or (a few states) Hveem stability.
sections.applicability: Applies when choosing the laboratory method to determine optimum micro-surfacing asphalt content.

sections.title: ISSA Procedure
sections.summary: The ISSA optimum-asphalt-content procedure graphically combines the Wet Track Abrasion Test (WTAT, ASTM D3910/ISSA TB-100) and the Loaded Wheel Test (LWT, ISSA TB-109) per Figure 4-3, targeting a residual asphalt content within 5.5-9.5%. WTAT sets the MINIMUM asphalt content from maximum allowed abrasion weight loss (1-hour or 6-day soak); LWT sets the MAXIMUM asphalt content from maximum allowed sand adhesion (flushing limit).
sections.body: The optimum asphalt content is determined from ISSA procedures by graphically combining the results of a WTAT and a loaded wheel test (LWT). Figure 4-3 (a, b, and c) shows how the optimum asphalt content along with an acceptable range is determined by graphically combining WTAT and LWT data. Ensure the minimum and maximum asphalt content falls within the range usually provided in the specification. The ISSA recommends that residual asphalt content be within a range of 5.5 to 9.5 percent. Wet Track Abrasion Test (ASTM D3910/ISSA TB-100): This test determines the abrasion resistance of micro-surfacing mixture relative to asphalt content and is one of two ISSA tests used for determining optimum asphalt content. This test simulates wet abrasive conditions such as vehicle cornering and braking. A prepared and cured sample of mixture 6 millimeters (0.24 inch) thick by 280 millimeters (11.0 inches) in diameter that has been soaked for periods of either 1 hour or 6 days is immersed in a 25 degrees C (77 degrees F) water pan and is wet abraded by a rotating weighted (2.3-kilogram [5.1 pounds]) rubber hose for 5 minutes. The abraded specimen is dried to 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) and weighed. The maximum allowed weight losses for 1-hour and 6-day soaks are 0.54 kilogram per square meter (0.11 pound per square foot) and 0.8 kilogram per square meter (0.16 pound per square foot), respectively. Asphalt contents that result in these weight losses are considered the minimum asphalt contents. The WTAT on a 6-day soaked sample is not required; however, due to the increased severity of the 6-day soak, it is preferred by laboratories and user agencies for predicting the performance of the system. Loaded Wheel Test (ISSA TB-109): This test is used to determine the maximum asphalt content to avoid asphalt flushing in micro-surfacing systems. This is accomplished by specifying and measuring fine sand that adheres to the sample subjected to simulated wheel loadings. The ISSA recommends a maximum sand adhesion value of 0.54 kilogram per square meter (0.11 pound per square foot) for heavy traffic loadings. If the sand adhesion is below this maximum value, mixture bleeding does not occur. In this test, a 50-millimeter-wide (1.97-inch-wide) by 375-millimeter-long (14.76-inch-long) specimen of desired thickness (25 percent thicker than the coarsest particle) is fastened to the mounting plate and is compacted with one thousand 57-kilogram (125.6-pound) cycles at 25 degrees C (77 degrees F). At the end of compaction, the specimen is washed, and then dried at 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) to a constant weight. A measured quantity of sand is then placed on the sample, and the LWT is repeated for a specified (usually 100) number of cycles. The specimen is then removed and weighed. The increase in weight due to sand adhesion is noted.
key_points: ISSA procedure graphically combines WTAT and LWT results (Figure 4-3) to find optimum asphalt content within a target 5.5-9.5% residual asphalt range.
WTAT (ASTM D3910/ISSA TB-100) sets the MINIMUM asphalt content: max weight loss 0.54 kg/sq m (0.11 lb/sq ft) for 1-hour soak, 0.8 kg/sq m (0.16 lb/sq ft) for the preferred 6-day soak.
LWT (ISSA TB-109) sets the MAXIMUM asphalt content (flushing limit): max sand adhesion 0.54 kg/sq m (0.11 lb/sq ft) for heavy traffic.
WTAT specimen: 6 mm thick x 280 mm diameter, wet-abraded 5 min by a 2.3 kg rotating rubber hose at 25 C.
LWT specimen: 50 mm x 375 mm, compacted 1,000 cycles at 57 kg/25 C, then loaded with sand for a further (usually 100) cycles.
figures: Figure 4-3: Determination of Optimum Asphalt Content
sections.applicability: Applies when using the ISSA WTAT/LWT graphical procedure to set the optimum (and min/max acceptable) asphalt content for a micro-surfacing mix.

sections.title: Marshall Procedure (Modified CRD-C649 or ASTM D6927)
sections.summary: A modified Marshall procedure (adapted for cold, polymer-modified emulsion systems) sets optimum asphalt content: air-cure at least 3 days, oven-dry 18-20 hours at 60 degrees C (140 degrees F), compact at 135 degrees C (275 degrees F) with 50 blows per side, targeting 4.5-5.5% VTM; specimens are tested for bulk specific gravity (ASTM D2726), stability, and flow. For thin micro-surfacing applications, stability is not treated as a primary factor; VTM requirements are adjusted for aggregate surface characteristics to hit target flow values.
sections.body: The Marshall HMA mixture criteria is used to determine the optimum asphalt content. Since these are cold polymer-modified emulsion systems, the stability and flow test procedures have been modified to allow for air and low temperature drying (at least 3 days of air curing, 18 to 20 hours of drying in an oven at 60 degrees C (140 degrees F) before compaction at 135 degrees C (275 degrees F)). The mixes are usually compacted with 50 blows per side. Under this procedure, several test specimens are prepared for combinations of aggregate and asphalt content. The asphalt contents are selected to provide VTM of 4.5 to 5.5 percent. The compacted test specimens are tested for the bulk specific gravity (ASTM D2726), stability, and flow values. Finally, the optimum asphalt cement content is determined using results from these tests. For thin micro-surfacing applications, the stability is not considered a primary factor in determining the optimum asphalt cement content. The surface characteristics of aggregates require adjustments in the VTM requirement to achieve the desired flow values.
key_points: Modified Marshall cure/compaction sequence: >=3 days air cure, 18-20 hr oven dry at 60 C (140 F), compact at 135 C (275 F), 50 blows/side.
Target VTM is 4.5-5.5%; specimens are tested for bulk specific gravity (ASTM D2726), stability, and flow.
For thin micro-surfacing, stability is not a primary factor; VTM is adjusted for aggregate surface characteristics to reach target flow.
sections.applicability: Applies when using a modified Marshall procedure to determine optimum asphalt content for a micro-surfacing mix.

sections.title: Design Limitations
sections.summary: ISSA cohesion torque has no established field-performance correlation and shows reproducibility issues (30- vs. 60-minute pass/fail inconsistencies, subjective visual torque-failure calls); WTAT is field-correlated only for 6 mm/Type 2 gradation, and limestone can pass the 1-hour soak but fail the 6-day soak; the LWT has known reproducibility problems and can over-predict allowable binder for some aggregates; and Marshall's low-void design target does not match observed field voids (10-15% after 1-2 years) -- a cold Marshall variant is under development to correlate better.
sections.body: ISSA Design: Torque values are measured in the laboratory under specific conditions; no correlation has been established with pavement performance in the field. Perform the mixing and wet cohesion test at various moisture contents, relative humidity, and temperatures to simulate the expected field conditions. In addition, it has been reported that aggregates that met ISSA torque standards for 60 minutes have failed to meet the torque values for 30 minutes. Laboratories also use a subjective analysis to determine torque; the sample is examined after the torque is applied, and if it fails, the torque value is determined from a visual examination of the condition of the sample, which negates the objectivity of the cohesion test. The WTAT was correlated to field performance for only 6-millimeter (0.24-inch) thickness and Type 2 gradation; accordingly, values of 0.54 kilogram per square meter (0.11 pound per square foot) are not used for other thicknesses and aggregate gradations without further verification. Also, limestone materials meet the WTAT standard for 1-hour soak periods but fail to meet maximum abrasion loss when a sample with a 6-day soak is tested. The reproducibility of the LWT is questionable: the arm that moves the wheel does not stay horizontal during the test, changing the pressure on the sample; the weights used to apply pressure are bags of lead shot that shift during the test and affect the applied pressure; sample preparation has been shown to affect LWT results by a factor of as much as two; the test specimen flushes if water levels are not carefully controlled; and for some aggregates the LWT permits excessive binder, resulting in unacceptable mixtures, particularly in high-shear areas such as intersections. Marshall Design: The applicability of this HMA test for micro-surfacing is questionable. Micro-surfacing mixtures do not reach the low void content levels seen during Marshall design; field observation has noted air voids of 10 to 15 percent after 1 to 2 years of placement. A cold Marshall test procedure has been developed by one materials laboratory to better estimate and correlate with actual field voids.
key_points: ISSA cohesion torque values are not field-performance correlated and show reproducibility gaps (60-min pass vs. 30-min fail) and subjective visual torque-failure calls.
WTAT's 0.54 kg/sq m (0.11 lb/sq ft) limit is field-validated only for 6 mm thickness/Type 2 gradation; limestone can pass the 1-hour soak but fail the 6-day soak.
LWT reproducibility issues: non-horizontal arm travel, shifting lead-shot weights, sample-prep sensitivity (up to 2x result variation), water-level-driven flushing.
LWT can over-predict allowable binder for some aggregates, causing unacceptable mixtures in high-shear areas like intersections.
Marshall's low-void design target does not match observed field voids (10-15% after 1-2 years); a cold Marshall variant is being developed to correlate better.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting ISSA/Marshall micro-surfacing test results with awareness of their known field-correlation and reproducibility limitations.

sections.title: Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Remove all loose material and repair structurally deficient areas before applying micro-surfacing; clean and seal cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in) or containing vegetation.
sections.body: Ensure the pavement surface has all loose material removed prior to application of the micro-surfacing material. Repair any structurally deficient pavement areas. Clean and seal cracks wider than 3 millimeters (1/8 inch) or filled with vegetation prior to application of the micro-surfacing.
key_points: Remove all loose material and repair structurally deficient areas before micro-surfacing.
Clean and seal cracks wider than 3 mm (1/8 in) or containing vegetation.
sections.applicability: Applies to surface preparation immediately preceding micro-surfacing placement.

sections.title: Application
sections.summary: Apply a tack coat, then fog the surface damp (no free water) just before micro-surfacing; minimum thickness must exceed the aggregate's maximum nominal size (usually 1.25-1.5x that size), about 10-13 mm (3/8 to just over 1/2 in); wheel ruts deeper than 6 mm (1/4 in) get a separate rut-fill layer first; emulsion is typically heated to 27-49 degrees C (80-120 degrees F) before mixing; the system opens to traffic within about 1 hour. A test section is important (quick-set system, field vs. lab variability); nurse trucks enable continuous placement, and longitudinal joints get a 50 mm (2 in) overlap.
sections.body: Apply a tack coat to the pavement surface prior to application of the micro-surfacing. Immediately prior to application, wet the pavement surface with a water fogging. This fogging leaves the surface damp but with no free water. Ensure the minimum thickness of micro-surfacing material application at least exceeds the maximum nominal size of the aggregate in the mixture (usually 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 times the maximum nominal size). This relates to minimum thicknesses of from 10 to 13 millimeters (3/8 to slightly over 1/2 inch). Where wheel ruts exceed 6 millimeters (1/4 inch) in depth, place a separate rut-filling layer prior to the complete overlay. The emulsion is usually heated to within 27 to 49 degrees C (80 to 120 degrees F) prior to mixing. Micro-surfacing applications are designed to be opened to traffic within 1 hour after placement. Temperature and humidity are the controlling factors for curing micro-surfacing after placement. As the temperature increases and the humidity decreases, the cure time decreases. Construction of a test section is very important for micro-surfacing due to changes in field conditions from lab conditions. Micro-surfacing is a quick-set system; therefore, changes or variations in field conditions require moisture, additive, or basic mix design changes to meet field conditions. Where possible, accomplish placement utilizing "nurse trucks" to allow for continuous placement. Nurse trucks are vehicles that are intended to carry aggregate, emulsion, and water to the application vehicle, whereby application of the micro-surfacing is a continuous operation. Whenever placement of the micro-surfacing is stopped, lift and clean the spreader box and ensure the transverse joint is squared. Paper strips or metal flashing is used to improve transverse joints. Construct longitudinal joints with a 50-millimeter (2-inch) overlap to assure complete coverage and to reduce rigid development. Use of an operator to control the rate of material flow along with careful control of the placement vehicle's speed allows for accurate placement of the micro-surfacing.
key_points: Apply a tack coat, then fog the surface damp (no free water) immediately before micro-surfacing placement.
Minimum thickness exceeds the aggregate's max nominal size (usually 1.25-1.5x that size), typically 10-13 mm (3/8 to just over 1/2 in).
Wheel ruts deeper than 6 mm (1/4 in) get a separate rut-filling layer before the full overlay.
Emulsion is typically heated to 27-49 C (80-120 F) before mixing; the system opens to traffic within about 1 hour.
A test section is important (quick-set system, field vs. lab variability); nurse trucks enable continuous placement, and longitudinal joints use a 50 mm (2 in) overlap.
sections.applicability: Applies to field placement procedure, joint construction, and traffic-opening timing for micro-surfacing.
